title: Die drei Glückskinder
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 70. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, thun, Rath, Thier/Unthier, Thürmen, todt, ward).
about: KHM 70, a merchant’s joke told three times over: a father leaves his sons a cock, a scythe and a cat, with the advice to carry them where such things are unknown, and each son duly sells an ordinary thing for a beast’s load of gold. Then, in its last paragraph, the tale turns into something stranger and colder, as a kingdom that has just bought a cat burns its own castle to the ground trying to be rid of her. Nothing in it is enchanted; everything turns on people who have never seen a thing before and are terrified of what they hear.

sentences.t: Ein Vater ließ einmal seine drei Söhne vor sich kommen und schenkte dem ersten einen Hahn, dem zweiten eine Sense, dem dritten eine Katze.
sentences.l: A father once had his three sons come before him and gave the first a cock, the second a scythe, the third a cat.
sentences.n: “vor sich kommen lassen” — lassen with a bare infinitive, where English needs “had them come.” A Sense is the long two-handed mowing scythe, not a hand sickle.

sentences.t: „Ich bin schon alt,“ sagte er, „und mein Tod ist nah, da wollte ich euch vor meinem Ende noch versorgen.
sentences.l: “I am already old,” said he, “and my death is near, so I wanted to provide for you yet before my end.
sentences.i: “I am old already,” he said, “and my death is near; so I wished to see you provided for before my end.
sentences.n: wollte here is a past of intention softened nearly to a wish — I had it in mind to. versorgen is to provide for, to see someone settled.

sentences.t: Geld hab ich nicht, und was ich euch jetzt gebe, scheint wenig werth, es kommt aber bloß darauf an, daß ihr es verständig anwendet: sucht euch nur ein Land, wo dergleichen Dinge noch unbekannt sind, so ist euer Glück gemacht.“
sentences.l: Money I have not, and what I give you now seems of little worth; but it depends merely on this, that you apply it sensibly: only seek yourselves a land where such things are still unknown, and your fortune is made.”
sentences.i: Money I have none, and what I give you now seems of little worth; but everything turns on your using it sensibly. Only seek out a country where such things are still unknown, and your fortune is made.”
sentences.n: “es kommt darauf an, daß…” = it depends on, everything turns on. Glück runs through this tale in both its senses at once, luck and fortune: the title’s Glückskinder are fortune’s children.

sentences.t: Nach dem Tode des Vaters gieng der älteste mit seinem Hahn aus, wo er aber hinkam, war der Hahn schon bekannt: in den Städten sah er ihn schon von weitem auf den Thürmen sitzen, und sich mit dem Wind umdrehen, in den Dörfern hörte er mehr als einen krähen, und niemand wollte sich über das Thier wundern, so daß es nicht das Ansehn hatte, als würde er sein Glück damit machen.
sentences.l: After the death of the father the eldest went out with his cock; but wherever he came, the cock was already known: in the towns he saw him already from afar sitting on the towers and turning himself with the wind; in the villages he heard more than one crow, and nobody would marvel at the creature, so that it had not the appearance as though he would make his fortune with it.
sentences.i: After the father’s death the eldest set out with his cock; but wherever he came, the cock was already known. In the towns he saw one from far off, perched on the steeples and turning with the wind; in the villages he heard more than one crowing; and nobody would wonder at the creature, so that there seemed no likelihood of his making his fortune with it.
sentences.n: The cocks on the Thürme are weathercocks on church steeples — the joke of the sentence. “es hatte nicht das Ansehn, als würde…” = it did not look as though; würde is subjunctive, holding the prospect unrealised. Thurm and Thier keep the archaic th of modern Turm and Tier.

sentences.t: Endlich aber gerieths ihm doch, daß er auf eine Insel kam, wo die Leute nichts von einem Hahn wußten, sogar ihre Zeit nicht einzutheilen verstanden.
sentences.l: At last, however, it did succeed for him, that he came to an island where the people knew nothing of a cock, and did not even understand how to divide up their time.
sentences.i: At last, though, he had the luck to come to an island where the people knew nothing of a cock, and did not even know how to divide up their time.
sentences.n: gerieths = gerieth es (modern geriet es); “es geräth mir” = it turns out well for me. eintheilen (modern einteilen) is separable, and here splits around zu: “ein-zu-theilen”.

sentences.t: Sie wußten wohl wenns Morgen oder Abend war, aber Nachts, wenn sies nicht verschliefen, wußte sich keiner aus der Zeit herauszufinden.
sentences.l: They knew well when it was morning or evening, but at night, if they did not sleep through it, none of them knew how to find his way out of the time.
sentences.i: They knew well enough when it was morning or evening; but at night, if they did not sleep it away, no one could tell whereabouts in the hours he was.
sentences.n: “sich herausfinden” = to find one’s way out — out of the undivided night, in this case. The phrase “sich aus der Zeit herausfinden” is odd in German too, and is meant to be. verschlafen = to sleep through, to sleep away.

sentences.t: „Seht,“ sprach er, „was für ein stolzes Thier, es hat eine rubinrothe Krone auf dem Kopf, und trägt Sporn wie ein Ritter: es ruft euch des Nachts dreimal zu bestimmter Zeit an, und wenns das letztemal ruft, so geht die Sonne bald auf.
sentences.l: “See,” spoke he, “what a proud creature: it has a ruby-red crown on its head and wears spurs like a knight; it calls to you three times in the night at a fixed hour, and when it calls the last time, the sun soon rises.
sentences.i: “Look,” said he, “what a proud creature — a ruby-red crown on his head and spurs like a knight’s. Three times in the night he calls out to you at a set hour; and when he calls the last time, the sun will soon be up.
sentences.n: The comb is a Krone and the leg-spurs are a knight’s Sporn: the sales pitch dresses an ordinary bird in nobility. anrufen (to call to) is separable — “ruft euch… an”; “des Nachts” is a genitive of time.

sentences.t: Wenns aber bei hellem Tag ruft, so richtet euch darauf ein, dann gibts gewiß anderes Wetter.“
sentences.l: But when it calls in broad daylight, then prepare yourselves for it: then there will certainly be other weather.”
sentences.i: But if he crows in broad daylight, then make ready for it — the weather is sure to change.”
sentences.n: “sich auf etwas einrichten” — to arrange oneself for something, to make ready for it; darauf points ahead at the daytime crowing. Wenns is wenn es, gibts is gibt es.

sentences.t: Den Leuten gefiel das wohl, sie schliefen eine ganze Nacht nicht und hörten mit großer Freude wie der Hahn um zwei vier und sechs Uhr laut und vernehmlich die Zeit abrief.
sentences.l: That pleased the people well; they did not sleep a whole night through, and heard with great joy how the cock at two, four and six o’clock called out the time loudly and distinctly.
sentences.i: This pleased the people well; they stayed awake a whole night through, and heard with great delight how the cock at two, at four and at six called out the hour loud and clear.
sentences.n: abrufen = to call out a time or a name, as a watchman does on his rounds — the bird is being sold as a town clock.

sentences.t: Sie fragten ihn ob das Thier nicht feil wäre und wieviel er dafür verlangte.
sentences.l: They asked him whether the creature were not for sale, and how much he demanded for it.
sentences.i: They asked him whether the creature was for sale, and how much he wanted for it.
sentences.n: feil = for sale, an old word that survives in modern feilbieten, to offer for sale.

sentences.t: „Etwa so viel, als ein Esel Gold trägt,“ antwortete er.
sentences.l: “About as much as a donkey carries in gold,” answered he.
sentences.i: “About as much gold as a donkey can carry,” he answered.

sentences.t: „Ein Spottgeld für ein so kostbares Thier“ riefen sie insgesammt und gaben ihm gerne was er gefordert hatte.
sentences.l: “A mocking-price for so precious a creature,” they cried all together, and gladly gave him what he had demanded.
sentences.i: “A trifling sum for so precious a creature!” they cried with one voice, and gladly gave him what he had asked.
sentences.n: Spottgeld — literally “mockery-money”, a price so low it insults the goods. insgesammt = modern insgesamt. The 1857 text leaves the exclamation without any closing mark before riefen, and we keep its punctuation.

sentences.t: Als er mit dem Reichthum heim kam, verwunderten sich seine Brüder, und der zweite sprach „so will ich mich doch aufmachen und sehen ob ich meine Sense auch so gut losschlagen kann.“
sentences.l: When he came home with the riches, his brothers marvelled, and the second spoke “then I will set myself out too, and see whether I can knock my scythe off as well.”
sentences.i: When he came home with the riches his brothers were astonished, and the second said: “Then I too will set out, and see whether I can turn my scythe to as good account.”
sentences.n: “sich aufmachen” = to set out (separable auf-). losschlagen is a dealer’s word: to knock a thing off, get it off one’s hands at a good price.

sentences.t: Es hatte aber nicht das Ansehen danach, denn überall begegneten ihm Bauern und hatten so gut eine Sense auf der Schulter als er.
sentences.l: But it had not the appearance for it, for everywhere peasants met him and had a scythe on the shoulder just as well as he.
sentences.i: But it did not look promising, for everywhere he met peasants with a scythe on the shoulder as good as his own.
sentences.n: “so gut… als er” = just as much as he did; modern German would use wie rather than als here.

sentences.t: Doch zuletzt glückte es ihm auch auf einer Insel, wo die Leute nichts von einer Sense wußten.
sentences.l: Yet at last it succeeded for him too, on an island where the people knew nothing of a scythe.

sentences.t: Wenn dort das Korn reif war, so fuhren sie Kanonen vor den Feldern auf, und schossens herunter.
sentences.l: When the corn was ripe there, they drove cannon up before the fields and shot it down.
sentences.i: When the grain was ripe there, they brought cannon up before the fields and shot it down.
sentences.n: auffahren, of artillery, is to bring the guns up into position; it is separable — “fuhren… auf”. schossens = schossen es. Korn is grain in general, wheat or rye, never maize.

sentences.t: Das war nun ein ungewisses Ding, mancher schoß drüber hinaus, ein anderer traf statt des Halms die Ähren, und schoß sie fort, dabei gieng viel zu Grund, und obendrein gabs einen lästerlichen Lärmen.
sentences.l: That was an uncertain thing: many a one shot over it, another hit the ears instead of the stalk and shot them away; much went to ruin in the doing, and on top of that there was an ungodly noise.
sentences.i: It was a chancy business: one man would overshoot, another would hit the ears instead of the stalk and blow them away; much was ruined in the doing, and on top of it all there was an ungodly din.
sentences.n: “zu Grund gehen” = to be ruined, to perish. lästerlich is properly “blasphemous” and here just means outrageous, ungodly. Lärmen is an older form of Lärm, noise.

sentences.t: Da stellte sich der Mann hin und mähte es so still und so geschwind nieder, daß die Leute Maul und Nase vor Verwunderung aufsperrten.
sentences.l: Then the man placed himself there and mowed it down so quietly and so swiftly that the people flung mouth and nose wide open with astonishment.
sentences.i: Then the man took his stand and mowed it down so quietly and so swiftly that the people gaped with astonishment.
sentences.n: “Maul und Nase aufsperren” = to gape open-mouthed, literally to fling mouth and nose wide — a coarse, comic idiom. niedermähen is separable: “mähte… nieder”.

sentences.t: Sie waren willig ihm dafür zu geben was er verlangte, und er bekam ein Pferd, dem war Gold aufgeladen, so viel es tragen konnte.
sentences.l: They were willing to give him for it what he demanded, and he got a horse; onto that one gold was loaded, as much as it could carry.
sentences.i: They were willing to give him for it whatever he asked, and he got a horse, loaded with as much gold as it could carry.
sentences.n: dem restarts the clause from Pferd with a dative demonstrative — onto that one gold was loaded — where English would use a relative pronoun or a participle.

sentences.t: Nun wollte der dritte Bruder seine Katze auch an den rechten Mann bringen.
sentences.l: Now the third brother too wanted to bring his cat to the right man.
sentences.i: Now the third brother wished likewise to bring his cat to the right buyer.
sentences.n: “an den rechten Mann bringen” = to find the right buyer for a thing; the phrase is still current German.

sentences.t: Es gieng ihm wie den andern, so lange er auf dem festen Lande blieb, war nichts auszurichten, es gab aller Orten Katzen, und waren ihrer so viel, daß die neugebornen Jungen meist im Wasser ersäuft wurden.
sentences.l: It went for him as for the others: so long as he stayed on the firm land, nothing was to be accomplished; there were cats in all places, and there were so many of them that the newborn young were mostly drowned in the water.
sentences.i: It went with him as with the others: so long as he stayed on the mainland nothing could be done. There were cats everywhere, and so many of them that the newborn litters were mostly drowned.
sentences.n: “es geht mir wie…” = it fares with me as with… “war nichts auszurichten” — sein plus zu plus infinitive makes a passive of possibility: nothing was to be accomplished. “ihrer so viel” is a genitive, “so many of them”.

sentences.t: Endlich ließ er sich auf eine Insel überschiffen, und es traf sich glücklicherweise, daß dort noch niemals eine gesehen war und doch die Mäuse so überhand genommen hatten, daß sie auf den Tischen und Bänken tanzten, der Hausherr mochte daheim sein oder nicht.
sentences.l: At last he had himself ferried across to an island, and it happened luckily that there not one had ever yet been seen, and yet the mice had so taken the upper hand that they danced on the tables and benches, whether the master of the house might be at home or not.
sentences.i: At last he had himself ferried over to an island, and it happened luckily that no cat had ever been seen there, while the mice had so got the upper hand that they danced on the tables and benches, whether the master of the house was at home or not.
sentences.n: “überhand nehmen” = to get out of hand, to become rampant. “der Hausherr mochte daheim sein oder nicht” — mochte here has the force of “might”, making the clause concessive: be he at home or not.

sentences.t: Die Leute jammerten gewaltig über die Plage, der König selbst wußte sich in seinem Schlosse nicht dagegen zu retten: in allen Ecken pfiffen Mäuse und zernagten was sie mit ihren Zähnen nur packen konnten.
sentences.l: The people lamented mightily over the plague; the king himself did not know how to save himself against it in his castle: in all the corners mice whistled and gnawed to pieces whatever they could get hold of with their teeth.
sentences.i: The people lamented mightily over the plague; the king himself could find no defence against it in his own castle. In every corner mice squeaked and gnawed to pieces whatever their teeth could seize.
sentences.n: “sich nicht zu retten wissen” = to be at a loss how to save oneself. The prefix zer- in zernagen means “to pieces”, as in zerbrechen, zerreißen.

sentences.t: Da fieng nun die Katze ihre Jagd an und hatte bald ein paar Säle gereinigt, und die Leute baten den König das Wunderthier für das Reich zu kaufen.
sentences.l: Then the cat began her hunt and had soon cleaned out a couple of halls, and the people begged the king to buy the wonder-beast for the kingdom.
sentences.i: Then the cat began her hunt, and had soon cleared a couple of halls; and the people begged the king to buy the wonder-beast for the realm.

sentences.t: Der König gab gerne was gefordert wurde, das war ein mit Gold beladener Maulesel, und der dritte Bruder kam mit den allergrößten Schätzen heim.
sentences.l: The king gladly gave what was demanded — that was a mule laden with gold — and the third brother came home with the very greatest treasures.
sentences.n: aller- intensifies a superlative: allergrößten, greatest of all. The three payments in turn are a donkey’s load of gold, then a horse’s, then a mule’s.

sentences.t: Die Katze machte sich in dem königlichen Schlosse mit den Mäusen eine rechte Lust und biß so viele todt daß sie nicht mehr zu zählen waren.
sentences.l: The cat made herself a right pleasure with the mice in the royal castle, and bit so many dead that they were no more to be counted.
sentences.i: The cat made fine sport with the mice in the royal castle, and bit so many to death that they were past counting.
sentences.n: “todt beißen” = to bite to death — the same make-it-so construction as “todt machen”, to kill. “nicht mehr zu zählen” is again sein plus zu plus infinitive: not to be counted.

sentences.t: Endlich ward ihr von der Arbeit heiß, und sie bekam Durst: da blieb sie stehen, drehte den Kopf in die Höhe und schrie „miau, miau.“
sentences.l: At last it grew hot to her from the work, and she got thirst: then she stopped, turned her head up into the height and cried “miau, miau.”
sentences.i: At last she grew hot from the work, and thirsty; so she stopped, turned her head up and cried: “Miaow, miaow.”
sentences.n: “stehen bleiben” = to stop, to stand still. The cry that follows is the whole hinge of the tale: it is only a cat being thirsty.

sentences.t: Der König sammt allen seinen Leuten, als sie das seltsame Geschrei vernahmen, erschraken und liefen in ihrer Angst sämmtlich zum Schloß hinaus.
sentences.l: The king together with all his people, when they perceived the strange crying, took fright and ran in their terror one and all out of the castle.
sentences.i: The king and all his people, when they heard the strange cry, took fright and ran in their terror every one of them out of the castle.
sentences.n: sammt = modern samt, together with; sämmtlich = modern sämtlich, all of them to a man. “zum Schloß hinaus” pairs zu with hinaus to mean “out through”, which English has to unpack.

sentences.t: Unten hielt der König Rath, was zu thun das beste wäre; zuletzt ward beschlossen einen Herold an die Katze abzuschicken und sie aufzufordern das Schloß zu verlassen, oder zu gewärtigen daß Gewalt gegen sie gebraucht würde.
sentences.l: Below, the king held council on what would be the best to do; at last it was resolved to send off a herald to the cat and to summon her to leave the castle, or else to expect that force would be used against her.
sentences.i: Down below, the king held council as to what were best to do; at last it was resolved to dispatch a herald to the cat, summoning her to quit the castle, or else to expect that force would be used against her.
sentences.n: “Rath halten” = to hold council. gewärtigen = to await, to expect something unwelcome; the whole sentence is written in the language of a chancery, as if the summons of a besieging army were being drafted against a cat.

sentences.t: Die Räthe sagten „lieber wollen wir uns von den Mäusen plagen lassen, an das Übel sind wir gewöhnt, als unser Leben einem solchen Unthier Preis geben.“
sentences.l: The councillors said “rather will we let ourselves be tormented by the mice — to that evil we are accustomed — than give our life up as prey to such a monster.”
sentences.i: The councillors said: “We had rather let the mice torment us — we are used to that evil — than give up our lives to such a monster.”
sentences.n: “lieber… als” = rather… than, with the comparison stretched right across the interjected clause. “Preis geben” (modern preisgeben) = to abandon, to give up as prey. Unthier = modern Untier, a monstrous beast.

sentences.t: Ein Edelknabe mußte hinauf gehen und die Katze fragen „ob sie das Schloß gutwillig räumen wollte?“
sentences.l: A noble page had to go up and ask the cat “whether she would vacate the castle willingly?”
sentences.i: A page of noble birth had to go up and ask the cat whether she would quit the castle of her own accord.
sentences.n: An Edelknabe is a boy of noble family serving at court. Grimm puts the reported question inside quotation marks, as though the herald’s words were being delivered verbatim, and keeps the question mark inside them.

sentences.t: Die Katze aber, deren Durst nur noch größer geworden war, antwortete bloß „miau, miau.“
sentences.l: But the cat, whose thirst had only grown greater still, answered merely “miau, miau.”

sentences.t: Der Edelknabe verstand „durchaus, durchaus nicht,“ und überbrachte dem König die Antwort.
sentences.l: The noble page understood “absolutely, absolutely not,” and carried the answer to the king.
sentences.i: The page understood it as “absolutely, absolutely not,” and carried the answer back to the king.
sentences.n: The joke is in the sound: “miau, miau” heard as “durchaus, durchaus nicht”, flatly and flatly no. Nothing in this tale is enchanted — everything turns on people hearing what they are already afraid of.

sentences.t: „Nun,“ sprachen die Räthe, „soll sie der Gewalt weichen.“
sentences.l: “Well then,” spoke the councillors, “she shall yield to force.”

sentences.t: Es wurden Kanonen aufgeführt und das Haus in Brand geschossen.
sentences.l: Cannon were brought up and the house shot into flames.
sentences.i: Cannon were brought up and the house set ablaze with shot.
sentences.n: “in Brand schießen” = to set alight by shooting at.

sentences.t: Als das Feuer in den Saal kam wo die Katze saß, sprang sie glücklich zum Fenster hinaus; die Belagerer hörten aber nicht eher auf, als bis das ganze Schloß in Grund und Boden geschossen war.
sentences.l: When the fire came into the hall where the cat sat, she sprang luckily out through the window; but the besiegers did not leave off any sooner than until the whole castle had been shot into ground and soil.
sentences.i: When the fire reached the hall where the cat sat, she leapt safely out of the window; but the besiegers did not leave off until the whole castle was shot to the ground.
sentences.n: glücklich here is “safely, by good luck” rather than “happily” — the tale’s Glück once more, and the cat keeps hers while the kingdom loses everything it has. “in Grund und Boden” is a fixed pair meaning utterly, to the ground. The tale simply stops there, with the buyers ruined and no comment from the teller.
